name: Carla Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm a sports reporter at the Eastport Evening Post, which is the regional paper and website for the coast. My main job is following Eastport Athletic, the football club, plus the rowing club, the youth leagues and anything else people care about at the weekend. A normal week is a training ground visit, a press conference on Thursday, and then Saturday afternoon in the press box with a pie going cold beside my laptop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being trusted by the people around the club. The kit man, the groundskeeper, the parents at youth matches, they tell me things because I've been turning up for five years. I grew up two streets from the ground, so it doesn't feel like a job some days.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Writing forty little results paragraphs for the Sunday league round-up. And the comments section, which can be vicious after a loss. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy up those results lists, because a couple of people on the news desk swore by it, and it does save me an evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's done what it was always going to do, tidy up the results lists. At work I'd joke that the robots still can't tell offside from onside. Online I'd mostly post about football, not this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. Sport is one of the reasons people still pay for the Eastport Evening Post, and the editor knows it. My savings are good and my boyfriend Rui has steady work as a carpenter, so the next few years look settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the tool for the Sunday results. Rui and I would keep saving for the wedding in two summers' time, at St Anne's, where my parents married. I'd maybe ask to cover the women's team properly, because that's growing and nobody here does it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really, because it means I keep a job I grew up wanting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. Is there anything about money or the paper that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The Post had cuts a few years ago on the subs desk, but sport was left alone because our pages get the most readers. I've got about eight months of costs saved and a share in my grandmother's old house, so I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the women's team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because their crowds have doubled in two years and the coverage hasn't. Families take their daughters, and those girls deserve to see a proper match report in the paper. It's also good for me, because it's a patch nobody else owns yet.

say: I'd say AI did what it was always going to do: tidy up **results lists**.
I'd joke at work that robots still can't tell **offside from onside**.
think: I think sport is one reason people **still pay** for the Post.
With good **savings** and Rui's steady carpentry work, the next few years look settled.
do: Keep using the AI tool for the **Sunday results** round-up.
Keep saving for the **wedding** at St Anne's in two summers.
Ask to cover the **women's team** properly.
feel: I'd feel **calm** and happy to keep a job I **grew up wanting**.
S0.quote: Sport is one of the reasons people still pay for the Eastport Evening Post, and the editor knows it.
fieldNote: Carla's security comes from **sport's pull** on readers, plus savings and her partner's steady trade.
She uses AI **only for chores**, after colleagues proved it worked.
She spots a **new patch**, the women's team, as a way to grow her role.

steps.text: Keep covering Eastport Athletic and pitch regular women's team match reports
Keep saving with Rui for the wedding at St Anne's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the computers can do the results, but nobody wants a match report from something that wasn't there. I'd probably say it to the sports editor, Dave, quite firmly. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the round-ups and the quick match reports go first, and that's maybe a third of what I write. There are already services that turn a stats feed into a football match report in seconds. The paper might keep one sports reporter for the big club and let the rest be software, and I'm not sure I'd be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, since half the desk would already be using them, and I'd make myself the person who checks the automated reports. I'd push hard into interviews and features, the stuff that needs me at the training ground. I'd also look at getting my coaching certificate at the youth club, partly as a backup and partly because I'd enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got savings and Rui, but I'd feel the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else on the desk would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kevin, who's been doing cricket and darts for twenty years. Kevin's in his fifties and writes exactly the kind of short reports that software can copy. He's a good man and he's got grandchildren, and I'd hate to watch him be pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, that's not up for debate. We might put the house hunting off a year, though, and keep living in the flat above Rui's workshop until I know where I stand.

say: I'd say nobody wants **a match report** from something that wasn't there.
I'd tell **Dave**, the sports editor, firmly, but stay quiet online.
think: I think round-ups and **quick match reports** go first, about a third of my work.
The paper might keep **one sports reporter** for the big club, maybe not me.
do: Learn the tools and become the one who **checks** automated reports.
Push into **interviews and features** that need me at the training ground.
Start a **coaching certificate** at the youth club as a backup.
feel: I'd feel **anxious** but not panicked, with savings and Rui behind me.
S1.quote: There are already services that turn a stats feed into a football match report in seconds.
fieldNote: Carla expects the cut to fall on **routine reporting** first and knows she does a lot of it.
She'd learn the tools once **the desk** has proved them, which fits her steady nature.
Her marriage is **fixed**, but she'd delay house hunting by a year.

steps.text: Learn the desk's AI tools and check every automated match report
Start a youth football coaching certificate at the local club
Put off house hunting by a year and stay above Rui's workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening too fast and families are being left to sort it out alone. I'd probably say we need proper training places, not handouts. I'd say that at church as much as at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the Post shrinks to almost nothing in two years. My job is all phones, laptops and words, so the robots coming later don't help me at all. Rui's carpentry has those extra three years, so for a while he'd be keeping us both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd cut the wedding to something small at St Anne's with family only, and keep the money we'd saved. I'd finish my coaching certificate as fast as I could and ask the youth club about paid hours, because coaching kids is hands-on and people want a real person there. I'd also start helping Rui with the business side of the workshop, quotes and customers, though I know that's thinking work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I was losing the thing I'd spent my whole twenties building, and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about Rui keeping you both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange. My mum and dad both worked, and I always pictured us as equals. I'd accept it for a while, but I'd want to be earning again within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum the wedding is getting smaller but the marriage isn't. She'd cry, then she'd start ringing round to borrow chairs for the church hall.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and families are left to sort it out alone.
I'd say we need **training places**, not handouts, at church and at work.
think: I think the Post **shrinks to almost nothing** in two years.
My job is **all thinking work**, so the robots coming later don't help me.
Rui's **carpentry** has three extra years, so he'd keep us both for a while.
do: Cut the wedding to a **small family service** at St Anne's.
Finish the **coaching certificate** quickly and ask about paid hours.
Help Rui with **quotes and customers** at the workshop.
feel: I'd feel **alarmed**, losing what I'd built through my twenties.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum the wedding is getting smaller but the marriage isn't.
fieldNote: Carla sees her partner's **hands-on trade** as the household's buffer for about three years.
She moves toward **coaching**, which keeps a person in the room.
Being kept by Rui **sits uneasily** with her picture of an equal marriage.

steps.text: Hold a small family-only wedding at St Anne's and keep the savings
Finish the youth coaching certificate and ask for paid hours
Rely on Rui's carpentry income while I find new work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people are sensible about it. At work I'd tell younger reporters to start thinking about a second skill. I'd sound calmer than I felt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see the end of my reporting job coming around 2031. But five years means I could stay at the Post for three, save, and move into coaching or club work before it hits. Rui's workshop would have until about 2034 before robots matter, which gives us a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the big wedding plans, because we'd have time to pay for it. I'd save more, maybe an extra two hundred a month, and do my coaching badges over two seasons. In year three I'd talk to Eastport Athletic about a role in their community programme, which runs football sessions in schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control. Knowing AGI is five years away is like knowing a storm is coming next week rather than tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the community programme be safe from AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, I think, because you need someone on a pitch with twenty eight-year-olds. The paperwork would go to the computer, sure, but the coaching wouldn't, at least not until the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound calmer than you felt. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't like making a fuss. My dad always said you keep your worries at home. But inside I'd be counting the months.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to get ready** if people are sensible.
I'd tell younger reporters to start on **a second skill**.
think: I think my **reporting job** ends around 2031.
Rui's workshop has until **about 2034**, which gives us a cushion.
do: Save an extra **two hundred** a month.
Ask Eastport Athletic about its **community programme** in year three.
feel: I'd feel **anxious but in control**, like a storm coming next week, not tonight.
S3.quote: Knowing AGI is five years away is like knowing a storm is coming next week rather than tonight.
fieldNote: Carla keeps worries **private**, following her father's advice, so her public calm hides real concern.
She counts on the **robot delay** for both her coaching plan and Rui's workshop.
With time she'd keep the **full wedding**, unlike in the fast picture.

steps.text: Save an extra two hundred a month for three years
Earn youth coaching badges over the next two seasons
Apply to Eastport Athletic's schools community programme in year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out. I'd tell the youth club parents to think about what their kids are studying. I'd probably post a little about it, more than I usually would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels comfortable for me. I'd be 37, probably with a child or two, and I'd have had a full decade to save and build up coaching. The hard part would be the robots in 2039, when even coaching and Rui's carpentry start to feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for most of the decade and get properly good with the AI tools, because they'd be part of the job by then. I'd build up the coaching slowly, a session or two a week. Rui and I would put some savings into a small rental flat, so there's income that isn't tied to either of our jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mainly about the robots at the end. The AGI part feels like something I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a rental flat rather than other savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's something you can see and touch. My grandmother's house has been in the family for forty years, and that's the kind of security my family understands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands as well as their heads, so that if one goes they still have the other.

say: I'd say ten years is **fair warning** and nobody should be caught out.
I'd tell youth club parents to think about **what their kids study**.
think: I think ten years feels **comfortable** for me, at 37 with a full decade to prepare.
The hard part is **robots in 2039**, when coaching and carpentry feel it too.
do: Keep reporting and get properly good with the **AI tools**.
Build up **coaching** to a session or two a week.
Buy a small **rental flat** with Rui for extra income.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy**, mostly about the **robots** at the end.
S4.quote: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands as well as their heads, so that if one goes they still have the other.
fieldNote: Carla trusts **property** she can see and touch, like her grandmother's house.
Her real worry shifts to **2039**, when robots reach hands-on work.
Ten years lets her **plan around** AGI rather than react to it.

steps.text: Use the Post's AI tools daily on match reports and features
Coach youth football one or two sessions a week
Buy a small rental flat with Rui using joint savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose the job I grew up wanting, just before the wedding, and the only thing holding us up would be Rui's workshop. What would help is proper training places for people like me, paid while you learn, so it's work and not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it means for the clubs. A lot of small clubs survive because the local paper writes about them and sponsors read it. If nobody writes about the under-twelves, I'm not sure the local bakery keeps paying for their football shirts.

headlineQuote: If nobody writes about the under-twelves, I'm not sure the local bakery keeps paying for their football shirts.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old sports reporter** on a coastal regional paper, engaged to Rui, a carpenter.
She's **traditional and steady**, using AI for chores once colleagues proved it worked.
She feels **secure** if AI stalls, and anxious once routine reports get automated.
Under **fast AGI** she shrinks the wedding and leans on Rui while she retrains as a coach.
With more time she saves, earns **coaching badges** and buys a small rental flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her reporting job just before the wedding.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training places** so people can learn while earning, rather than relying on handouts.
